speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take all your four cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While SIAC draws a strong demand for arbitration from parties in Asia, there are trends and developments that indicate that the demand for arbitration in Singapore will move beyond Asia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Last year, the field of arbitration in Singapore was given a further boost to widen its global influence through the opening of Maxwell Chambers Suites with a whole suite of arbitration offices and facilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dignitaries from 12 countries and more than 350 guests from various facets of the legal industry attended the official opening.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It houses the local offices of top international dispute resolution institutions, such as the International Chamber of Commerce's International Court of Arbitration (ICC) as well as the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, at this point to declare for the purposes of this Committee of Supply (COS) debate, this cut and all cuts after this, that I am a lawyer whose practice covers arbitration, litigation, advisory work and intellectual property (IP).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: INSOL International is the International Association for restructuring, insolvency and bankruptcy professionals.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister share with us how the Ministry plans to help Singapore as a legal services hub, drawing to Singapore	the	demand	for	international	legal	services across key practice areas?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To further these objectives, our civil, community and family justice systems have gone through several refinements.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Launched in 2017, the State Court's Community Justice and Tribunals System (CJTS) is an electronic case filing and management system which helps promote access to justice by allowing parts of the legal system to be accessed by lay persons online.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through it, claims at the Small Claims Tribunal may be filed and negotiated, reducing the need to appear in Court where an e-settlement is reached.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Without needing to go to Court, neighbours can also try to resolve disputes with the help of a Court mediator through e-mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also passed the Protection from Harassment Act so that victims obtain protection from harassment more easily.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Minister elaborate on what has been and will be done to further enhance our civil, community and family justice systems?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, the criminal justice system is critical in maintaining law and order in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More than just a tool for ensuring that law be abided by and that there be order in Singapore, the criminal justice system is important for justice to be carried out, meted out in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The state has the proper mandate to mete out penal justice, punishing those who do wrong.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Otherwise, there may be increased vigilantism, mob justice and a descent into chaos and disorder.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The corollary of that mandate is preventing the injustice of punishing persons for wrongs they did not commit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Otherwise, the law may be seen as arbitrary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is, therefore, important that trust in our criminal justice system is maintained.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will the Minister, therefore, explain what has been done to ensure the continued efficacy of our criminal justice system here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although it is not my last cut for the COS, it is on a formidable fortress for IP, being Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Industrial Revolution 4.0 and the Digital or Information Age, rely heavily on intangible property rights, that is, IP rights, to protect the way systems are designed, codes are written, products are created.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: IP rights allow innovation to be sold, bought, traded and incentivises research and development (R&D) of technology.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: IP rights also allow businesses to protect their reputation and reap from investments made in the quality of their products and services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how the IP regime will be used as a means to help our companies remain competitive in a challenging global environment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, how will Singapore further fortify its position as a country and jurisdiction in which IP rights can be well protected and enforced?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, in a fast-changing and competitive global landscape, we do appreciate that one of a company's competitive advantages is its brand, ideas and innovations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore has come a long way in developing our IP capability and ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In fact, this is one of the reasons why Singapore is selected by many multinational corporations to invest their business and research development in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Intellectual Property Office of Singapore (IPOS) has been pushing the boundaries to support businesses in using IP to grow.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With IPOS’ strong reputation, credentials and capabilities in IP strategy protection and management, could the Ministry share how IPOS is helping Singapore companies, especially small and medium enterprises, understand the value of their IP, protect their IP and innovations, as well as leverage their IP for competitive advantage?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I welcome the Government’s move towards enhancing Singapore’s standing in becoming an even more established IP hub and the launch of IPOS International last August.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: IPOS can provide customised programmes, and this provides valuable assistance to many businesses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The use of technology by IPOS is also very encouraging.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Are Singapore small and medium enterprises (SMEs) actively leveraging the suite of tools and engaging IPOS International to better understand and develop their IP strategy for competitive advantage?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is MinLaw’s assessment of the progress that Singapore companies are making in leveraging IP for their business growth and the commercialisation of IP of Singapore companies?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, could the Minister also touch on what has been done to improve our criminal, civil, community and family justice systems to make access to justice for citizens simpler and more affordable?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Could the Minister also inform us on the key priorities in enhancing access to justice that we look forward to?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the law does allow for legal recourse to be provided to consumers who have been cheated by contractors who do not perform their duties to the required standard, there are cases where my residents have been let down or shortchanged by contractors who have done shoddy work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may not be altogether satisfactory, as the services rendered may be due to poor workmanship or left unfinished.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If the contractor, despite being given reasonable time, does not rectify the works, what it leaves the consumer to do is to have to hire another contractor to rectify the works and then obtain legal redress which might take some time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In one of the cases that my resident has sought my assistance, the said contractor has cheated others.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When she made a Police report, she was told that the Police could not assist and that they had to pursue their own cases.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The concern is that as they did this, besides recovering the money, whether the contractor was continuing to cheat others.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would also like to request the Ministry to share on what steps are being taken to educate and inform the public of their legal relief, especially in cases where Singaporeans do not have the financial wherewithal to afford legal representation and, hence, would be less cognisant of their legal rights.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By its very nature, the law can be intimidating to navigate for the common man.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To many, it can be dense or verbose and inflexible and jargon-laid.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How many of us have blindly clicked on compliance boxes or lengthy forms when we download the latest version of whatever software we need, or even signed Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) forms without reading them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, does the way companies and commercial entities and even the Government seek consent in today's digitalised world ensure that our people are informed about their rights, the rights they are giving up or responsibilities and obligations they are signing up to?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One Ministry whose website and mobile site have caught the eye for excellent legal design and user friendliness is that of the Ministry of Manpower (MOM).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Their mobile site is intuitive and captures all the critical information citizens will access in a simple and easy to read format.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I was made to understand from a public officer at MOM that there is a team that analyses user behaviour with a view to improve online interaction and how to make online services easily understandable and easily understood.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, the Budget Book lists the key performance indicators of the Ministry, some of which include a sound and progressive legal framework and access to justice for the low-income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the tech-related outcomes in our march towards digitalisation may more appropriately come under the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) or the Smart Nation Office, legal design inputs can help many other Ministries and Statutory Boards improve the delivery and quality of services, and ultimately, outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Ministry plays a part with legal design tools to make the law more easily understandable and understood by the layman.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Chair, my first cut is on the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) judgments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having a deeper understanding of the rulings of the ECT would benefit not just practitioners and lawyers, but claimants and respondents, too, when presenting their respective cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: ECT now has jurisdiction to adjudicate both salary-related disputes as well as wrongful dismissal claims, making it more convenient for parties to resolve employment disputes via a single forum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, an ECT judgment that is not satisfied would still need to be enforced in the same manner as an order made by a District Court.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This would involve detailed processes set out in the Rules of Court pertaining to the filing of relevant forms/documents as well as the payment of Court fees.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: A worker who has successfully obtained a judgment may thus still be subject to a protracted enforcement process.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For civil Court proceedings, even though registration for such legal aid can now be done online, a full means-test with a means-test officer is required if representation in Court proceedings is required.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Depending on the urgency of the case, it appears that it can take between seven days and a month to get an appointment and, thereafter, another appointment for statement-taking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest giving applicants the option to do means-testing as well as submit copies of required documents online in advance.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS), similar measures, such as allowing for registration and the means-test to be done online, can also be implemented to speed up the application process for CLAS cases.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Further, a central online legal aid portal can be set up.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Depending on whether legal aid is required for civil or criminal proceedings, potential applicants can then be directed to the relevant organisation’s website and resources.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This would make it easier and less confusing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Similarly, can the means-test to qualify for CLAS consider similar factors, such as those used with the new means-test administered by the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB)?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The concern becomes even more pertinent when it involves matters, such as those relating to divorce, applications under the Mental Capacity Act or criminal matters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, what has been done to improve the legal aid schemes to enhance access to justice?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could the Ministry look at how to further assist individuals who are not eligible for legal aid to get the help they need?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I declare that I am a lawyer in private practice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I raised previously the need to incentivise low bono efforts by lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many lawyers are already doing pro bono work but this often comes at a cost to the lawyer’s earnings, and thus not sustainable.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I had asked if a framework could be developed to support low bono efforts by lawyers to augment existing legal aid schemes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note from the response last year that MinLaw is working with partners like the Law Society Pro Bono Services and the Singapore Academy of Law to study how it could enhance support for pro bono and low bono efforts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could MinLaw give an update on these efforts?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I still get feedback on cumbersome processes from people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One example is Mr Chan, whose wife recently died intestate suddenly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is a caregiver of his autistic son aged 16.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on the current rules under the Probate and Administration Act, there was a need for him to get another person to agree to be a co-administrator to administer his late wife's estate to protect his minor son's interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In comparison, he was appointed as a single deputy by the Court to take care of his son and deal with his son's property and affairs under the Mental Capacity Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the Government has been reviewing this matter since 2017.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will also be grateful if the Government could please consider the interplay between the various statutes in its review, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Separately, I had pushed for Singapore to accede to the Hague Apostille Convention so as to rationalise the process involved in legalisation of documents for use here and in other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update on this matter.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I think mediation is a good dispute resolution mechanism for commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I had once personally participated in a mediation under the auspices of the Singapore Mediation Centre (SMC) as my firm was involved in a commercial dispute that resulted in litigation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I was, at the time, quite impressed with the mediation format.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was less contentious and driven by parties instead of lawyers to seek a win-win solution where both parties are in a position to accept.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It also makes sense from a commercial perspective.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mediation is more efficient than litigation in terms of time and cost.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There is no need for commercial entities to be distracted from their day-to-day businesses by being embroiled in long drawn out and costly litigation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This House has also passed the Singapore Convention on Mediation Bill earlier this month.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We could be one of the first signatories to ratify the Convention.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This means that almost seven in 10 commercial disputes referred to mediation are resolved amicably.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is a reflection of the good work that SMC puts in to resolve a majority of the disputes referred to them.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: If more litigated commercial disputes are referred to mediation, this could also potentially reduce the caseload burden of the Singapore Courts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: On the arbitration front, the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) has also seen a steady rise of cases over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It, therefore, appears to me that Singapore is well-placed to capitalise on these developments and resources to position ourselves as a leading global dispute resolution hub.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, Sir, I invite the Minister to share with this House the Ministry's larger strategic plans to promote Singapore as a leading global dispute resolution hub to resolve international cross-border commercial disputes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: This scheme is supposed to prepare law practices for future disruptions beyond baseline technology adoption, empower them to focus on delivering enhanced legal services, strengthen their capabilities and increase their competitiveness in the global landscape.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Law firms, like other businesses, need to equip themselves with the necessary technology to be efficient and productive and be ready for trends and changes in the future.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, as I had highlighted in my speeches in previous years, there is often hesitation on the part of small firms to invest time to review and adopt new technology because, unlike bigger firms, they cannot afford to dedicate resources and time to this effort in the midst of continuous and ongoing legal work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I am also not sure if awareness of the various support programmes and schemes is high amongst the lawyers in the smaller firms.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you can do both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Technology is increasingly being felt in the legal fraternity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: AI and machine learning have already been tapped to review contracts and conduct research in other countries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I submit that existing stakeholders in the legal sector, such as practising lawyers and inhouse legal counsel, will also need to be brought up to speed in this global move towards adopting legal technology solutions to improve productivity, accuracy as well as enhancing access to justice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is inevitable that technology will continue to disrupt and change current work processes in law firms as well as the legal departments in the organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Funding of legal technology implementation and solutioning as well as training and upgrading subsidies should thus be set aside for continuing legal education in this area of legal tech solutions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest that such funding should be extended to all relevant stakeholders in the legal sector, including inhouse legal departments and counsel of private companies and organisations as well as the public agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Para-professionals, commonly known as paralegals, are invaluable to the legal industry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are employed by law firms as well as the legal departments in private companies and public agencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Depending on the needs of the employer, a paralegal's role can range from conducting research and managing routine files to even knowledge management.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding the wide scope of responsibilities undertaken by paralegals, their professional development as well as interests and welfare are often not given due priority, save for the Chief Justice's recent mention of the increasingly important role of allied legal professionals trained in skillsets relevant and complementary to the core responsibilities of a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I submit that more can be done to encourage employers of paralegals to set out clear career progression options for paralegals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These could include more diverse roles, such as project management, business development, legal innovation and legal technology, as well as understanding foreign legal jurisdictions to enable internationalism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: To help paralegals take on such roles, a skills framework, backed up by both the industry and regulators with nationally endorsed training providers, must be promulgated and made available to all paralegals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Further, an association or union can be specifically set up to better engage paralegals, look after their interests as well as facilitate their professional training, development and progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This must come with support from the industry and regulators.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Would the Minister elaborate on how we can optimise state properties to meet social and community needs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How can we optimise state properties to meet social and community needs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank the Members for their speeches and for the queries that they have raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw's mission is, broadly, two-fold: first, to continually update our legal framework to meet both today's and tomorrow’s needs; second, to work together with our stakeholders to strengthen Singapore's position as a leading international legal services hub for Asia and, of course, the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the past two years, we had passed many pieces of legislation to achieve these objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have redoubled our efforts at establishing Singapore as a legal services hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has included, as Mr Sitoh Yih Pin has said, the signing of the Singapore Convention on Mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will touch more on that in a moment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our focus for the coming year will be to implement the changes that we have put in the place, to ensure also that every Singaporean can be confident of effective access to justice in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our legal system must be user-friendly, affordable and provide effective solutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It must also be accessible to the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will, therefore, continue to grow the legal services sector to ensure that more can enjoy the benefits of this growth whilst at the same time ensuring that those who require and need those services will have access to those services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, Ms Jessica Tan and several others have touched on this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those who use the family justice system are usually in a state of emotional turmoil, mental anguish and have seen their families break up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is not a legal proceeding that they wish to be in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are often also vulnerable, especially those families with children, whose interests, above all, must be looked after.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is the design focus of our laws – to look after the children in any matrimonial or family proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This awareness has driven our revamp of the family justice system since 2014, as Members would be aware.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our aim is to reduce time, cost and, perhaps most importantly, unnecessary acrimony and to recognise and protect the interests of the children, so that the acrimony does not affect and adversely weigh on the outcomes for the children.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have moved significantly to improve the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are encouraging numbers, but we do want to go further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The committee was tasked to look beyond just legal proceedings and, instead, focus on designing a robust ecosystem of support for families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The committee made recommendations on mental capacity issues to address the needs of our ageing population as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are working with our stakeholders to implement these recommendations and put them into place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Jessica Tan spoke about the enforcement of maintenance orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an important concern and we do not want someone to have to spend time running from pillar to post to try to recover something that the Court has already granted by way of an order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have taken steps, however, over the years to address this issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where the spouse cannot find work, perhaps due to poor health or other reasons as a reason why the orders have not been fulfilled, we should recognise that support services rather than legal proceedings will provide more effective relief for the wife and the children concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nevertheless, at the same time, our laws must also have the tools to deal with a spectrum of options, different situations, including imprisonment, if necessary, so that we can enforce and give teeth to orders that have been made in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But, overall, Members should be assured that where there are genuine financial difficulties, circumstances that the family faces, the Courts will more likely order mediation or financial counselling to find a solution rather than to just simply impose the hard law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay also suggested that in the case of insolvent companies, or companies that either cannot or have been unable or refuse to pay the wages, that MOM could advance money to the worker and thereafter stand in his place as a preferred creditor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I understand that MOM has looked at this proposal before and Mr Patrick Tay will probably know that while doing so might well help that specific worker in the immediate short term, it may also inadvertently create a larger problem of a viable company defaulting or owing the salaries in knowledge that the workers could find an alternative avenue to obtain those payments using Government funds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These provide ex-gratia payments to low-wage employees whose employers were unable to pay salaries due to financial difficulties or business failure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On the publication of certain ECT decisions, Mr Patrick Tay would know that, today, ECT judgments or grounds of decision are available to the public upon request.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Because the original proceedings in the first place under the statute are held in private to protect the confidentiality of the parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, it follows that whatever takes place in those proceedings is not reported as of right.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But the ECT will assess requests for either the judgments or the grounds of decision and, where appropriate, such as when it would help future cases or there is strong precedential value, then those would become available.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I understand that MOM also makes applications to the ECT to publish judgments or grounds of decision that become useful reference points for parties in the same vein as I have outlined.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this, we have worked closely with the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and other stakeholders in the past two years to make wide-ranging amendments to both procedural and substantive criminal law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Much legislation has been passed in this House on this aspect over the past two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In particular, the Penal Code amendments have kept our legislation apace with emerging crime trends developing here and around the world and strengthened protection, in particular, for vulnerable victims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This year, my Ministry is supporting the work of the newly-formed Criminal Procedure Rules Committee chaired by the Chief Justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This committee will ensure that the Court procedure remains nimble and also adaptable to adjust and meet evolving needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Ms Jessica Tan asked about supporting the efforts of Singapore enterprises to thrive in an innovation-driven economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the interest of time, let me just highlight a few.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This identifies intangible assets that are critical to the companies' businesses and recommends how to report them in a way that best communicates the business value of these intangible assets to their investors and the market, obviously, to try to realise the full value of such intangible assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, IPOS' subsidiary, IPOS International, helps enterprises develop strategies to protect, manage and also commercialise the intangible assets and IP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To date, IPOS International has helped about 100 enterprises, with close to 95% of them being SMEs and startups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is in answer to Ms Jessica Tan's question as to what help has been given to companies in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has also developed a series of IP management business guides, which around 1,000 enterprises have accessed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Around 70 enterprises have used IPOS International's diagnostic tool, illuminate® for enterprise, to assess their IP and intangible asset risks and gaps, and perhaps they will be working on them and, eventually, can also take advantage of IDEAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This supports the development of innovative AI technologies and helps companies with these technologies to remain competitive ahead of the curve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as we know, technology sometimes gets outmoded very quickly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, the quicker we can deal with the patent applications, the more value it is to the companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To date, over 150 businesses have used the IPOS Go app to protect their brands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These points would also be of interest to Mr Pritam Singh who asked about design processes and systems with the end-user in mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One change we have implemented is the increased flexibility to grant aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Applicants who do not satisfy the means criteria but are otherwise unable to afford basic legal services without causing significant hardship to themselves and their families, these persons may have their applications reviewed by an independent Means Test Panel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Previously, the moment an applicant failed the means test, then the application was rejected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Now, we look at whether or not this person has failed it only because he had circumstances that might cause hardship to himself or to his family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The panel may waive the means criteria for these deserving applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The grant of aid will, of course, still be subject to the merits test, to ensure that applicants have good reasons to bring or defend their cases in law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked about improving service delivery for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will do so through a number of key initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we have just launched the revamped Applicant Portal for civil legal aid and new features will be included over the next few weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When completed, this portal will do away with the need to appear in person to complete the means testing and also the statement-taking so that it can be done remotely without having to make a trip to the office.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It reduces the need for applicants to provide information that the Government already has.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, for a start, we will tap on MyInfo to provide personal details and income information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It also, at the same time, is two-way, allowing the applicants to check on the status of their application and be updated as to its progress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will be able to provide basic legal information to LAB's potential applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will also be able to triage them based on the nature of their case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And in most cases, this will save the applicants a trip to LAB to discuss it with the case officers in person.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Potential applicants can use these documents to self-help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They do not have to go to see lawyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With iLab, these simple standardised documents commonly used can be generated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We hope to launch this in the next few weeks.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think these are all features which fit towards that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it is a good reminder by Mr Pritam Singh that we should be looking at the various enhancements to ensure that they are designed around our clients' needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I take the point that it ought not be dense or verbose, and we will endeavour to avoid that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Putting information online, enabling online applications, making it two-way, the process being dynamic, will make it easier for our clients who may find it difficult to be away from their families or take time away from work.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also undertook three rounds of rigorous user testing with LAB clients on the Portal and also on iLAB because we recognise that it can also be very frustrating if it does not work, the portal is not intuitive and not interactive enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we have been fairly rigorous in the way which we have tested it before it goes out to market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The broader legal system also designs access to justice and legal awareness with the end-user in mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Courts have pioneered an online dispute resolution system which litigants-in-persons can use to conduct negotiations and mediation for claims online for the Small Claims Tribunal (SCT).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin would be glad to hear that as well – you can now mediate your case online as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we are also exploring new features, such as asynchronous hearings to make it more convenient for Singaporeans to resolve their disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, rather than to have parties at the same time at the same place, these facilities make it easier, facilitate claims before the SCT and also allow for some mediation to take place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I shall elaborate more closely on the law firms' adoption of technology, a point raised by Ms Rahayu Mahzam, later in my speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes will simplify and, therefore, shorten the application process while, at the same time, maintain the rigour of the means test which we need to have, given that these are public funds that are being used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will be working with the Law Society Pro Bono Services (LSPBS), which administers CLAS, to implement the changes in the coming year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Despite these changes, I wish to assure Members of this House that there will be no material impact on the number of households eligible for criminal legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also continue to support the efforts of LSPBS to improve the administration of CLAS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes using technology to make the application process more efficient and user-friendly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At this juncture, let me acknowledge the strong support of members of the Bar, without whom the scheme would not have been quite so strong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Sixteen law firms have also signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOU) to pledge to take on CLAS cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I thank the lawyers, the legal fraternity for their support of this programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked about support for Singaporeans who cannot qualify for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To do so, we continue to forge strong partnerships with stakeholders to provide affordable legal help.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, even if you cannot qualify for these programmes, what else do we do?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We work with LSPBS, the legal fraternity and our community partners to provide legal help through Community Legal Clinics and various legal literacy and legal assistance programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Government also works with the Law Society and the Law Schools to cultivate a strong pro bono culture within the legal profession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, law students are exposed to pro bono work from an early stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They have structured internships with LAB to inculcate not just the spirit but also to allow us to tap on the law students to assist in our pro bono programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There have also been efforts by the wider legal ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Singapore Academy of Law will be launching a collaborative workspace called "CLICKS @ State Courts", which will help firms adopt technology by providing them with shared amenities and facilities, such as meeting rooms and office equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And by reducing operational costs, firms can then consider providing accessible and affordable legal services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But I think Ms Rahayu Mahzam will agree with me when I say that access to justice goes beyond legal aid and just providing low bono or pro bono services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is equally important that we see access to justice as understanding the problems in daily life, understanding at what stage there should be legal, and perhaps also social intervention, so that we can provide simple yet effective and, as far as possible, long-lasting solutions to the problem at hand and not just fix the surface, leaving the underlying problems to continue to rear its ugly head.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Cases will be heard by specially trained judges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Volunteers will be on hand to assist victims, including from a social aspect and not just from a legal aspect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These changes are intended to minimise anxiety and stress, and to ensure that the victims of harassment can obtain effective remedies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continue to monitor its effectiveness as part of the broader framework that we have to resolve community disputes and also study areas for improvement of the processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, I would stress that mutually agreed solutions between two neighbours, for instance, should always remain the first port of call, that is, should always be the first base that one goes to instead of triggering a process in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CDRT, as far as possible, should be a measure of last resort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we encourage Singaporeans to engage their neighbours in an amicable manner, when disputes arise – use community mediation services, use grassroots leaders who can facilitate the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On community mediation, I should stress that the approach has been effective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, the Government is also reviewing the processes and requirements for the application of probate and letters of administration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for an update on this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Amongst other things, we are considering digitalising the process, in sort of the same fashion that I have been outlining, to make it simpler, easier and faster, and linking up Government systems to facilitate the retrieval of information.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the end of the day, information has to come through so that the applications can be processed and that, sometimes, is a chokepoint.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we will work on digitalising the process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And also streamlining the legal requirements imposed on applicants.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These, I believe, will improve the experiences of Singaporeans dealing with end-of-life issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But even as we streamline, we must be careful that the law will continue to protect the interests of beneficiaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is one area where the original stakeholder or perhaps owner of the assets is not around to say how it should be done or what his intentions were.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But within this rubric, strike an appropriate balance so that we can look out for the interests of both the convenience of the parties applying as well as also the rigours of what the interests of the beneficiaries ought to be.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will provide more details in the coming year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have seen one or more of these types of individuals at some stage and it is frustrating.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) which Mr Lim Biow Chuan can share more information on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: CASE publishes a Consumer Alert List on its website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That is a useful first port of call.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It lists companies that have multiple complaints made against them and operates to warn consumers about contractors with poor track records.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, to those cases that Ms Jessica Tan has spoken about where there have been repeated cases, it ought to be on this list.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If not, we will try and find a way to better police it so that members of the public can be warned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If there are unfair practices, for example, false and misleading claims and so on, CASE may refer the matter to the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCCS) for further action under the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where an amicable settlement is not possible even with CASE's assistance, consumers can file claims with SCT.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SCT provides a forum that is low-cost, no lawyers are involved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And SCT may order one party to pay money to another party arising from these claims and also order a party to make good on deficiencies, as in the Member's example, the construction contract, for instance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving on, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Sitoh Yih Pin spoke about strengthening Singapore's position as a premier international legal services and dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members will know that we are constantly looking at how we can enhance this, what we can do, what other spaces we can fill or other opportunities there will be for the Singapore brand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We look at what we can do to create value for our economy, what we can do to enhance Singapore's value-add as a business hub and, of course, ultimately, providing good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also want to support our people and businesses in exploiting these opportunities as far as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One area in which we shall move to keep pace with the competition is in the area of conditional fee agreements (CFAs).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are also promoting the use of Singapore law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, encouraging published research on areas of Singapore law that are relevant to commercial parties internationally, and finally, promoting standard forms, that is, use of straightforward, standard forms, governed by Singapore law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked about progress in dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore remains one of the leading hubs for dispute resolution in the world today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have flagship institutions that Mr Christopher de Souza mentioned providing a full suite of such services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have best-in-class hearing facilities at Maxwell Chambers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to strengthen that framework by supporting the ecosystem for viable international dispute resolution services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have various reviews underway, including a review of the International Arbitration Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I had earlier mentioned the Singapore Convention on Mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Yes, indeed, we were one of the first two countries, together with Fiji, to ratify the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This took place a few days ago in New York.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These efforts, not just to get the countries to sign and to ratify, but to promote more countries to come on board, have broader implications for Singapore's place in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is a powerful statement for multilateralism and has also enhanced our reputation in the international arena.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will build on the signing of the Convention last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will host a second annual Singapore Convention Conference in September this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be part of a week-long series of events related to international dispute resolution services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This conference and, indeed, the week, will continue to position Singapore as a thought leader in this field and also a forum that parties can choose to come to, regardless of whether the ultimate contract or the subject matter of their agreement is in Singapore or not, to choose Singapore as a forum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the area of civil cooperation, Mr Murali Pillai asked about the legalisation of documents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is a point that Mr Murali Pillai has raised several times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will include preparing the necessary draft legislation domestically in order to accede to the Convention, and thereafter, we will be in the position to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All these efforts will create opportunities for those in the legal sector and also for those who want to enter the legal sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this note, Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked what the Government is doing to support lawyers and law firms to exploit these opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we will be launching a Technology Innovation Roadmap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This roadmap is the product of intensive consultations with more than 80 stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include law firms, companies, law schools, research institutes and other Government agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will help Singapore law firms understand and embrace technology to improve productivity and the quality of their legal services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Altum Law Corporation is a five-lawyer strong Singapore law firm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the Tech Start for Law and the Tech-celerate for Law initiatives, MinLaw and the Law Society curated a shortlist of technology solutions and also vendors to help address common problems, common issues amongst smaller law firms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Grants to support up to 70% of adoption costs were available under the schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Strong efforts have been made to promote these schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Law Society reached out to at least 450 Singapore law practices through workshops and seminars to promote this programme and Altum was one of those who was a participant in these events.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They were able to upgrade from the standard suite of computer services – they were using Microsoft Office, I believe – to legal technology solutions that were more curated and were better suited to their needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Roadmap will include plans to help to continue to fund law firms, help them to understand what technology can do for their efficiency and also expand support to inhouse legal teams to adopt legal technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Patrick Tay mentioned, this reflects our belief that both those in practice as well as those in the inhouse role have much to benefit from adopting legal technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we will support the development of cutting-edge legal technology relevant to their work and also reform legal education to build a pipeline of tech-ready legal professionals to support the legal industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: More details will be announced later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will help such PMETs to exploit new opportunities that will be created.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Law Society and Workforce Singapore have developed a Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) to help employers hire and reskill mid-career PMETs to join the legal sector as paralegals or legal secretaries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Paralegals and support services do play an important role in Singapore's legal industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We note Mr Patrick Tay's suggestions and we will continue to work with the relevant stakeholders so that we can support this segment of the legal industry more closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The programme will expand the pool of Singapore lawyers who understand Chinese culture, the way in which business is done, the legal system and laws, are conversant with Mandarin in the legal context, and can also work with Chinese companies and law firms to better meet clients' needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is one element of the Ministry's strategy to help Singapore lawyers seize new opportunities in different jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA optimises land resources to support the economic and social development of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It plays a number of roles, including, as Mr Christopher de Souza outlined, optimising the use of state land and, of course, also developing Singapore's geospatial capabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA is intensifying its efforts to engage and collaborate with stakeholders, members of the public, on the interim use of vacant state land and properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, Members may be aware that SLA and the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) launched the Power-Up Pasir Panjang ideas competition in April 2019, and reached out to members of the public, professionals and students to co-create ideas for the Power District.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the coming weeks, SLA will also be launching engagements with stakeholders to rejuvenate the Old Kallang Airport.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is part of the Reinventing Spaces into Vibrant Places initiative that was launched with URA in 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The map will allow users to visualise Singapore in 3D.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will support the efforts of businesses and the public who require these services to have new platforms to support their services and products as well as also develop services for the community at large.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It will facilitate private sector access to 3D geospatial models and data on a restricted basis and, through this, we hope to encourage the private sector to experiment with innovative solutions and services for their customers and the general public using 3D geospatial models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Sandbox will enable SLA to obtain feedback from the private sector to enhance the experience and to improve the geospatial models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chairman, in conclusion, my Ministry will continue to ensure that Singaporeans continue to enjoy effective access to high quality justice – that is a fundamental – and also to build on Singapore's attractiveness as a legal services hub, ensuring that the benefit of the ensuing growth will be shared by more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Importantly, we do all this not on our own but through working closely with so many stakeholders – the bench, the bar, the legal industry, the universities, law students and the wider community – and for that, we are very grateful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: On my particular cut about Singapore being a leading international dispute resolution hub, one of the flagships we have, apart, obviously, from our Court system, is SIAC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Minister would know, my question is really a nuts and bolts on how we get the model clause out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In a model clause, there is the centre, there are the rules, there is the seat and there is Singapore law being the relevant law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, my question really is: how are we able to advance Singapore law, advance the seat of Singapore, through these clauses such that international parties come?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And when international parties come, they do not come with lawyers, they come with their experts, they come with their decision-makers and their witnesses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, how can we use that space to enhance Singapore law and Singapore as an international legal hub?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, having a model law is one thing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But what we want to do is to really build the ecosystem that supports why a party from outside Singapore will want to choose Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if I may summarise some of the points from my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our high-quality jurisprudence coming out of our Courts helps a lot in that regard for parties who want to choose Singapore law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Third, we want to look at the way in which our stakeholders – law firms, lawyers, those who practise here, those who practise abroad – are equipped with this information, so that when they do the negotiation, persons, such as yourself, Mr Christopher de Souza or Mr Murali Pillai, can then take these learning points, take these model clauses and persuade external parties that, in Singapore, we do not only have the best facilities, but we have the best, most neutral system that will ensure a fair adjudication of the disputes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think all of these parts must come together in order for us to build a first-class hub and continue to sustain that first-class international dispute hub.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, do you want to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I was hoping to ask for another clarification, but that is all right, I can withdraw the cut.

speaker: The Chairman
text: You have a few minutes to ask your further clarification.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: My next question is on a different cut, which is, Singapore as a formidable IP fortress.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think we can provide a lot of protection and enforcement, but how is IPOS and MinLaw working with the R&D outfits to ensure the commercialisation of IPs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, it is not only a portcullis or a fortress where we protect it but where we can enhance it into commercial terms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, at the baseline, that is always something that we look at, frankly speaking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We want to make sure that our laws are updated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, as I mentioned on several occasions and also earlier, we will look at enhancing and revising the Copyright Act, an experience that we have had after we did extensive consultations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What else can we say to people about how their ideas, their patents, their innovations will be better protected in Singapore and also enforced, should the case be necessary?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: How do you monetise the value in intangible assets, assets that would otherwise be difficult to look at in terms of valuation?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look at how it can be done so that we can help companies raise capital, raise financing and leverage the value of such intangible assets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When you bring all these together in the ecosystem, you will then have, in Mr Christopher de Souza's words, a formidable fortress, in which to not just register but enforce and eventually enjoy filing of the patents in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we provide the whole spectrum of services, that is when we can then go out there and tell the major companies, inventors and innovators of the world to come into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have the entire suite of services for you and, should there be any disagreement, any dispute over the services, they will be resolved in a firm, fair and completely aboveboard, neutral, rule-of-law fashion.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That assurance that we give to investors would be the best assurance we have in growing perhaps not just the IP sector but overall in our key development areas in Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, it is about three minutes before guillotine time, so you may have to withdraw.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I join my fellow parliamentarians in thanking the Senior Minister of State for his comprehensive responses and also all the hardworking officers in MinLaw and the various arms and bodies which report to MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With that, I seek your leave, Mr Chairman, to withdraw my amendment.
